metadata.description: Research queue for the Semantic Archaeology lexicon. Entries await independent verification before promotion to canonical.json.
metadata.root: Optional. Shared id linking entries descended from one root (e.g. 'dragan'); siblings wake together.

candidates.note: 'to drag, pull'; to draw a picture was to drag a stylus across a surface.
candidates.editorial_notes: Entry is for the picture sense, where 'pull' is buried; 'draw water/a sword' keeps it alive. Pairs with write 'scratch'. Kin: drag, draft/draught, dray. Sense date (~1200) unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

candidates.note: from Old English dragan 'to drag, pull': a pull of air, a pull of drink, a drawn-out sketch.
candidates.editorial_notes: Polysemy, not homonymy (filter correctly skipped it). 'Draft' is the phonetic spelling of draught; British keeps draught for air, drink, ships. Essay sense hides the pull best. Gloss untested in running text. Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

candidates.note: 'the two arms outstretched, an embrace'; a fathom was the span of a man's arms, then a depth measured in arm-spans, then to sound a depth, then to understand.
candidates.editorial_notes: Entry is for the verb 'can't fathom', where the arms are buried. Root *peth2- 'to spread out' (PIE) via Proto-Germanic *fathmaz. Kin: petal, patent, Latin patere 'lie open'; perhaps also Latin pandere 'to spread' (expand, pace, pass): that link is debated, see research_notes 2026-10-02. Gloss untested in running text. Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

Root *peth2- (PIE), with fathom and patent. Image may be thin: 'leaf' alone adds little; 'spread flat' is the point. Entered English via New Latin petalum (1700s). Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

candidates.note: 'lying open'; letters patent were royal grants issued unsealed, open for anyone to read. The inventor's patent is short for them.
candidates.editorial_notes: Root *peth2- (PIE), with fathom and petal; Latin patere 'to lie open' (as in mundus patet, verbum patet). Adjective 'patent' (obvious) keeps the openness alive; the noun hides it. Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

candidates.note: 'a row of bushes planted as a fence'; to hedge a bet (1600s) was to fence in one's losses, to hedge a statement to fence a claim with qualifiers.
candidates.editorial_notes: Entry is for the verb 'she hedged', where the thornbush is buried; the garden noun keeps it alive. Proto-Germanic *hagjo; root id 'hag' = Proto-Germanic *hag- 'enclosure'. Kin: haw/hawthorn, Dutch Den Haag. Deeper: perhaps PIE *kagh- 'to catch; wattle, fence' (Welsh cae, perhaps quay via Gaulish); unsourced, keep hedged. Self-describing: the lexicon's 'perhaps' rule is a hedge. Gloss untested in running text. Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.

candidates.note: haga 'enclosure, hedge' + þorn 'thorn': the thorn used for hedging fields.
candidates.editorial_notes: Sibling of hedge (root 'hag'). Low frequency; probably a family anchor more than a strong entry, though 'haw' alone is opaque to modern readers. Unchecked against etymonline and Wiktionary.
